chunks: Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Ubayd Allah narrated to me from his father, from his grandfather Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from his father Muhammad ibn Khalid, via his chain, raising it to 'Unbasah al-Ta'i, from Abi Jubayr, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: The head of Husayn, smeared with his blood, will be presented to Fatimah. She will cry out, 'O my son! O fruit of my heart!' The angels will cry out due to Fatimah's cry, and the people of Resurrection will call out, 'May Allah kill the killer of your son, O Fatimah.' Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will say, 'I will take revenge on him, and on his Shias, his lovers, and his followers.'

Indeed, on that day, Fatimah will be upon a she-camel from the camels of Paradise, with a prominent forehead, clear cheeks, and black eyes. Her head is of pure gold, and her necks are of musk and amber. Her rein is of green beryl, and her mounts are studded with jewels. Upon the camel is a howdah, its covering from the light of Allah and its filling from the mercy of Allah. Its rein is a farsakh of the world's farsakhs. Seventy thousand angels surround the howdah, glorifying, exalting, declaring oneness, proclaiming greatness, and praising the Lord of the worlds.

Then a caller will call out from the depths of the Throne, 'O people of Resurrection! Lower your gazes, for this is Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah.' She will pass over the Sirat. Fatimah and her Shias will pass over the Sirat like a flashing lightning bolt. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: And their enemies and the enemies of their progeny will be thrown into Hell.
ai.seo_question: What happens to Fatimah Zahra and her enemies on the Day of Resurrection according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-A’mal* vividly depicts the Day of Resurrection, where Fatimah al-Zahra (peace be upon her) mourns the martyrdom of Imam Husayn (peace be upon him) before the gathered humanity and angels, highlighting the intergenerational impact of Karbala on Shia eschatology. It elaborates on her celestial status through detailed descriptions of her ornate mount and radiant appearance, symbolizing her purity and high rank, while her followers cross the Sirat bridge swiftly like lightning. This narrative underscores the Shia belief in the eternal connection between the Ahl al-Bayt and their devotees, culminating in the ultimate triumph of the progeny and the defeat of their enemies.
